the development of stochastic methods for efficient and accurate prediction of the Thero-Hydro-Mechanic behavior of large containment structures.
the numerical modeling of concrete cracking and its effect on the tightness of large constructions.
the numerical simulation of the ThermoHydroMechanical (THM)-coupled behaviour of large concrete structures, such as nuclear vessels or containment buildings.

the proposed methodology allows to (a) efficiently compute the structural tightness of large containment structures (b) provide an accurate probabilistic assessment of the structural tightness under service conditions (c) identify the most influential input parameters in terms of tightness (d) provide a physical interpretation of the tightness behavior and its uncertainties (e) provide a physically relevant and cost-effective probabilistic assessment of structural tightness under the effect of service loads.
the methodology proposed here is efficient and effective for the prediction of the structural response of a large containment structure in terms of cracking pattern and tightness under service loads.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed an efficient and accurate probabilistic strategy for predicting concrete cracking and leakage of large structures under uncertainty.
we have developed a probabilistic methodology to assess the structural performance of concrete constructions with a containment role, such as dams, nuclear vessels or containment buildings.
we have developed a global stochastic approach to perform efficient probabilistic THM calculations of the dry air leakage rate of containment structures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is now possible to perform efficient probabilistic THM simulations of large structures with containment role, in particular for the assessment of their leakage rate.

we have developed an effective methodology to compute the probabilistic response of large structures under service loads in a reasonable time frame, using physically relevant and computationally efficient models.
we can predict with a good accuracy the leakage of a large structure (in this case the VeRCoRs building) using a stochastic methodology based on a physically representative damage model.
